📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there is perhaps nothing so brutal in a Total War game than getting an army full of elite units wiped out, and it appears that pain remains a factor in the upcoming Total War conversion of : Warhammer 40,000. Creative Assembly also has some nifty ideas around breaking the game into mini-campaigns for each star system you visit.

In an hour-long deep-dive livestream of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, developer Creative Assembly demonstrated the game in action, focusing initially on how armies navigate from planet to planet. Each star system apparently acts as a "contained campaign" you can hop between in the game.

The star system the stream focused on is Praevoss, a mid-sized collection of planets: three of which you can land on and fight on, while the others are smaller and unable to support your tactical warfare shenanigans. Once you're finished with a star system, you move on, carrying over units and unlocked skills.

"First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," Creative Assembly explained on the livestream. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start, [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do.".

One of the objectives highlighted in the livestream was an Ork Scourge, which required the player - controlling Space Marines - to hold the planet while eradicating the Ork presence.

Industry observers note that as you can imagine, much of the stream was dedicated to the fleet of spaceships at your disposal - fleet movement and management, and the abilities they provide to your armies such as orbital bombardments. There was also detail on how ships transport troops, as well as the upgrades you can build to further enhance their power.

Industry observers note that on the topic of transporting troops, the developers focused on the small number of expensive but powerful Space Marines they controlled. These Space Marine armies come with a potentially "devastating" cost if you mess up and lose your armies during one of the star system campaigns.

Recent findings suggest that "Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the developers explained. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that.".

Sources indicate that total War: Warhammer 40,000 is set to release some time in 2027, though no specific date has been established as of writing. Much has been seen at this point on its gameplay, galactic or otherwise. As we near the end of the year, fans are clamouring for official word on when they can take to the stars.

'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time.
  • In a recent development, now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox.
  • Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

In a recent development, now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro.".

According to recent reports, PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

It has been revealed that in the post, Rockstar also unveiled that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

Industry observers note that that's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar claims that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Industry observers note that again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the organization hasn't explained why that is.

The Nightingale First Look: Dakota and Elle Fanning on Their Long-Awaited First Film as Sisters

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when I spoke to Dakota and Elle Fanning last fall, they pondered what it would be like to work and live together while making The Nightingale, the film adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s best-selling novel about French sisters in Nazi-occupied France.
  • Now, more than a year later, the Fanning sisters tell me they needn’t have worried.
  • Hollywood has long been plotting to get the Fanning sisters in the same movie—and not as different versions of the same character, as they played in Dakota’s 2001 feature debut, I Am Sam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when I spoke to Dakota and Elle Fanning last fall, they pondered what it would be like to work and live together while making The Nightingale, the film adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s best-selling novel about French sisters in Nazi-occupied France. It marks the siblings’ first time acting opposite each other onscreen. “We’ve literally never done a scene together, ever,” Dakota said then, as Elle wondered if she’d get through their first take without breaking character: “Am I going to laugh? Better to get it out of your system now.”.

Now, more than a year later, the Fanning sisters tell me they needn’t have worried. “It was nerve-wracking to think, ‘How is this going to feel?’” indicates Dakota, who’s in Latest York to shoot an Apple TV series opposite Elle’s former Sentimental Value costar Stellan Skarsgård. “Our way of processing things that we’re both nervous about is to just not talk about it in an effort to downplay what could go wrong or be strange. So that’s what we did—and it was the easiest thing in the world. We played together our entire lives and acted out scenarios, so it felt like clicking back into that. Like, ‘Oh, of course, this is what we do.’”.

Hollywood has long been plotting to get the Fanning sisters in the same movie—and not as different versions of the same character, as they played in Dakota’s 2001 feature debut, I Am Sam. They were in talks to colead My Sister’s Keeper, a 2009 tearjerker about a young girl conceived to become a marrow donor for her gravely ill sister, but stepped away from it because Dakota didn’t want to shave her head. (Sofia Vassilieva and Abigail Breslin ended up in the movie.) Plus, as Dakota previously told me, she and Elle acting together at that age “would’ve been gimmicky.”.

Now, the Fannings say they felt ready to streamline their singular talents into one special project. “We never shied away from being together because we are so close, but we both feel properly established on our own,” says Dakota. “So getting to do things together, together, together is a real joy.”.

The Nightingale, which hits theaters on March 19, 2027, follows guarded older sibling Vianne, who urges caution when dealing with the Germans but later shields Jewish children in her home—and rebellious younger sister Isabelle, who joins the French Resistance and becomes a target of the Nazis. “What I love about it is it’s two women fighting, resisting,” Elle previously told VF. “One in a louder way, one in a quiet way.”.

Dakota and Elle were bound for preproduction in Budapest on The Nightingale as the pandemic hit in March 2020. “It has been a long time coming,” says Hannah, the book’s author. “These two young women have been attached to this project and been passionate about it for a very long time,” Hannah tells VF. “As the author, to have two female partners who were as dedicated to bringing this novel to screen in the way I saw it as well, felt like a remarkable gift.”.

Hannah, whose 2008 novel Firefly Lane was later adapted into a Netflix series starring Katherine Heigl and Sarah Chalke, notes she’s unlikely to ever adapt one of her own books for the screen. “I would be afraid that my love for the story that I had written would in some way limit me from being able to see what the film really needed to be.” But she was part of the script development process for The Nightingale with screenwriter Dana Stevens from the very start. “Nightingale has always been a very special book for me,” says Hannah. “And more importantly, it’s a very special book for my readers.”.

When the project was revived, the Fannings returned not only as stars, but producers through their Lewellen Pictures production banner. Filmmaker Michael Morris, fresh off the fourth Bridget Jones movie, stepped in to replace their original director, French actor Mélanie Laurent. Just as Bridget Jones was an opportunity to make a film about grief under the guise of romantic comedy, Morris saw The Nightingale as his chance to explore sisterhood through a sweeping World War II epic. “I saw these two women, how they exist independently in the world as complementary creatures,” says the director, who is also father to three daughters. “They are built from the same building blocks, but they’ve gone different ways.”.

Morris clocked a similar dynamic between his leads. “Elle is immediately outgoing and loud and can feel super funny making fun of herself. Dakota has all those qualities too, but can sometimes be very focused and funny in a sort of sly, quieter way,” he explains. “They fill up the spaces that the other one leaves for each other, like all really good siblings. I met with Dakota, and then I met with Elle, and by the end of the Elle meeting, I was like, ‘I totally understand this film.’”.

Of the more than 11 million copies of The Nightingale that have been sold worldwide, perhaps the most valuable belongs to Elle and Dakota’s grandmother, who, after reading the 2015 historical novel, told her granddaughters that they would be perfect for the parts of Isabelle and Vianne. “Vianne highlights her love through nurture and cooking and taking care of a home. Elle’s character, Isabelle, is the more obviously daring one that runs towards danger and adventure,” indicates Dakota. “I do think that we are truly probably the people to play these roles because we deeply understand that dynamic. We inhabit some of the same qualities.”.

It has been revealed that although presented with separate drivers at the start of production, Elle and Dakota rode to set for their joint scenes in the same car. “[The characters] are apart a lot of the time, so when we had scenes that were together, those were treated with a lot of care,” says Elle, speaking backstage from Today, where she promoted her role as a young Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games prequel. “Because it’s quite powerful to finally see them united and to see us on screen together.”.

In a recent development, their director states because Elle and Dakota had never acted opposite one another, they brought a vibrant, kinetic energy to each shared scene—an offering that Morris took seriously as the filmmaker to capture it. “We’re talking about women who are barely 30 who have been working at the highest level for 25 years. A quarter of a century spent on sets of really wonderful projects,” he explains. “So you have all this experience that they have that they can bring to bear in a moment. It’s like watching someone who’s incredibly talented at athletics. They look and function like normal people, and then you kick a football at them, and they suddenly do incredible things. Like, ‘Whoa, where did that come from?’”.

In a recent development, the Fannings left it all out on the field—and tried not to bring work home into their shared living space. “It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” notes Elle. “And also knowing that we’re representing these women from that time,” including Andrée de Jongh, a Belgian woman who was helping downed airmen escape from France during World War II, whose story Hannah says helped inspire her original novel. “Because there’s so much brain power [used] on set,” says Elle, at the end of each day “you have to just recharge and eat Thai food.”.

The sisters’ downtime involved a steady stream of true crime and Real Housewives, as well as Dakota’s first full-fledged watch of Elle’s Emmy-nominated Apple TV series Margo’s Got Money Troubles, released in the thick of The Nightingale’s filming schedule. “So what we do,” says Dakota, “my mom does this too, is when any of us has something that’s out, she turns on every TV in the house and leaves it playing, as she says, ‘For the views.’” Elle and Dakota each laugh, shaking their heads a little. “So I was doing that with Margo,” Dakota recalls. “I’d have it going on my iPad and my phone when they were sitting there charging. For the views.”.

Sources indicate that but they couldn’t block out their day jobs entirely. When Dakota had a day off, she, like her character Vianne, found herself picking up after her younger sister while she worked. “Her bed in the morning is like a tornado has run through it,” indicates Dakota. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”.

Edmund Donovan and Elle Fanning.

In a recent development, “It’s art imitating life,” says Elle, “because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed too.” By the end of the shoot, says Dakota, “it became a routine. I always made her bed like that when I could.”.

But the Fannings were fully aligned on the casting of their fictional father, calling Oscar-winner Mark Rylance their “dream casting,” from the beginning. “I always say he has twinkly eyes,” Elle explains. “We all know what an incredible actor he is, but to see it up close and get to act opposite that—it was really, really powerful.” Adds Dakota, “As a person and as an actor, you just feel his emotions and soul and heart on his fingertips [even] when he shakes your hand.”.

According to recent reports, morris thinks of Rylance’s character, Julien, an emotionally stunted World War I veteran, as the “third axis of a triangle—but he’s not just binding them together as sisters, he’s also tearing them apart because he’s not a healthy role model for most of their lives,” says the filmmaker. “Because Mark can be wonderfully lovable, we talked about what is it not to lean on that? What is it to be a bad parent? What is it to neglect? And it’s painful, but he doesn’t hide from the flaws of his character. He doesn’t try to make you love him.”.

The rest of the ensemble cast includes up-and-comers like Unorthodox breakout Shira Haas, All Quiet on the Western Front star Albrecht Schuch, and Civil War’s Edmund Donovan as Gaëtan, a communist resistance fighter and love interest for Elle’s character, Isabelle. The younger Fanning also enlisted a few of her costars on the Emmy-nominated Hulu series The Great for the film, including Douglas Hodge and Gwilym Lee, who plays Antoine, the soldier husband of Dakota’s character, Vianne. But “this is not a war movie,” Morris insists. “We are telling the story of real people from the POV of two young women living at the time. They’re not glued in on the grand sweep of history. They’re just living, trying to do the best they can. It’s not about the politics of the time, it’s about what you do about it. It’s a very contemporary film because I don’t know anyone who hasn’t grown up in a time when there isn’t something to get active about.”.

Hannah hopes that the film version of her novel will shed light on the fact that “so many of women’s vital historical stories have been lost or discounted,” adding, “Isabelle and Vianne, and in fact, many of the characters in this book risk their lives on a daily basis to fight for what they believe is right. And that’s a really important message at any time, now and throughout history.”.

Industry observers note that it wasn’t until their final week shooting the hotly anticipated adaptation that the Fannings got into something approaching a fight—while filming one of their favorite moments from the book, no less. “It really had nothing to do with the scene,” Dakota tells VF. “It was literally because we were on a couch that was too small for both of us. Elle had the comfortable position, and I was hanging off one side, uncomfortable and hot. And the way that I saw it is you are pushing me off.”.

It has been revealed that “Sabotage!” Elle interjects, wiping her morning-show makeup off mid-call with a mischievous grin. “I was like, ‘You’re sweating! Get this leg off of me.’ And Elle was like, ‘Stop talking to me.’ It was like a miniature explosion,” Dakota recalls with a laugh. “We both looked over at the crew, and they were grinning from ear to ear, like, ‘Finally, there it is.’ It was the closest thing that they had seen to a little disgruntledness from both of us.”.

That scene was also a favorite for Morris, who removed much of the script’s dialogue to focus on the dynamic between the sisters, both real and fictional. “Seeing these two women bring their entire life history as sisters to the moment, putting them that close together on this tiny couch, gave them no option but to be really close,” says Morris, who realized, “Oh, we need almost no words at all to tell the scene. Elle Fanning, Dakota Fanning, playing these sisters, brings us so much that we can just be there with them.”.

Hannah has yet to see the finished film, but is most eager to watch “the moment where Isabelle grabs her long braid and cuts her hair off in front of the Nazi officer to show her defiance, and her sister’s horror that she would be impulsive enough to do something like that and put them all in danger,” she tells VF. “I’m a little afraid to see the fullness of my vision through this film and how it will impact me. I have a feeling that I’m going to be crying like everybody else.”.

Sources indicate that nerves aside, Hannah is optimistic about the finished product after visiting The Nightingale set, where she walked through her characters’ childhood home, built from scratch, as dictated in the pages of her novel. “Down to the smallest detail, their vision was this magnification of my vision. Everything looked exactly as I had pictured it, and my research had defined it. Then to see Elle and Mark Rylance bring these characters to life in a way that even goes beyond what I am able to imagine was…” she trails off. “I guess the only word I can use really is magical.”.

Sources indicate that to hear the Fannings tell it, the experience was similarly profound. “Of course, we visit each other on sets, and I’ve seen her work,” says Elle, “but it’s very different to be looking at each other in front of a camera. It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer. Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”.

According to recent reports, “But we did really savor it,” Dakota replies. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything,” she claims, giving her sister a meaningful glance across the Zoom screen. “That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6's seismic launch has registered on a governmental level. A spokesperson for UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has hailed the game as a "British success story", but confirmed Burnham himself won't be playing it. His diary is apparently "very full".

"Rockstar Games is a British success story made in Edinburgh," a Downing Street spokesperson told The Independent - referencing the series' Scottish origins and ongoing development at Rockstar North - "and many fans are already saying GTA has been worth the wait." When asked if Burnham will be making time for GTA 6, the spokesperson responded: "His diary is very full. He won't be playing it.".

Downing Street went on to address the problem of teenagers potentially skipping school to play the game, emphasising that children "should be in classrooms" this week because "every day in school matters".

The leader of Labour's opposition, the Conservative party's Kemi Badendoch, recently expressed similar concerns. "I know people are worried about the game content," she wrote. "At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half-an-hour on it and then went out and did something else.".

It has been revealed that GTA 6's culture-shaking success was unlikely to pass without reference by the government, but the celebratory tone is a marked departure from Burnham's predecessor Kier Starmer calling Rockstar's firing of 34 staff last year "deeply concerning". We are awaiting a verdict in the resulting employment tribunal related to it.

This state recognition of GTA 6 is not without precedent. It wasn't long ago that French President Emmanuel Macron congratulated Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on its award-winning and heart-winning success. That game sold 8 million copies in one year; GTA 6 is estimated to have sold 25 million copies in one day.

GTA 6 has been hailed as a generational release - an exorbitantly luxurious game that "pushes back the horizon of video games", Chris Tapsell wrote in Eurogamer's GTA 6 review.

Industry News: 'Yellowjackets' season 4 review: A strong start but too many unanswered questions risk a 'Lost'-style ending

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (797 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For five years and three seasons, Paramount’s “Yellowjackets” has been at once enthralling and appalling audiences.
  • Industry observers note that what eventually roped me in and made it impossible to look away were the stellar performances from the massive ensemble cast and the storytelling that — cliché as it sounds — actually left me on the edge of my seat, peeking out in horror from behind my fingers.
  • In a recent development, heading into the show’s fourth and final season, though, those strengths become double-edged swords.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For five years and three seasons, Paramount’s “Yellowjackets” has been at once enthralling and appalling audiences. As someone who is easily squeamish, I’ll admit that when I first tuned in years ago, I almost abandoned the show altogether, too disturbed by watching teenagers hunt their friends like animals and decapitate corpses to continue.

Industry observers note that what eventually roped me in and made it impossible to look away were the stellar performances from the massive ensemble cast and the storytelling that — cliché as it sounds — actually left me on the edge of my seat, peeking out in horror from behind my fingers. Adding to that was “Yellowjackets’” knack for unveiling mysteries that left viewers, myself included, desperate for answers.

In a recent development, heading into the show’s fourth and final season, though, those strengths become double-edged swords. The major questions that kept audiences hooked for years now demand answers before the series finale. Likewise, the interwoven narrative — jumping between the teenage plane crash survivors stranded in the wilderness and their adult counterparts — has always been an effective tool, but before the end, these timelines need to find a satisfying cohesion.

Having watched the first eight of season 4's 10 episodes, I can safely and somewhat unfortunately say that while “Yellowjackets” satisfies in some areas, it falls short in others — and it doesn’t have much time left to course-correct.

In a recent development, easily the most compelling aspect of these first eight episodes is the exploration of the team’s return home. For three seasons, audiences knew these traumatized kids — the ones who survived, at least — would eventually make it back, with the adult timeline confirming several names (Shauna, Misty, and Melissa among them).

Prior to season 4, however, “Yellowjackets” had yet to reveal that exact moment of return and its immediate fallout: watching characters who hunted, killed, and ate their friends attempt to slip back into their “normal” lives. While the adult timeline already proved the survivors never truly moved past their ordeal, seeing their parent reunions, the jarring shift in high school social dynamics, and the strange fame that comes with surviving a mass tragedy is precisely what audiences have been waiting for.

With just two episodes to go, a shocking number of questions remain on the table, raising an obvious concern: has “Yellowjackets” saved too much for an epic finale? Of the many shows met with controversy over their endings, the mind-bending sci-fi series “Lost” is among the most notorious and perhaps the closest comparison to “Yellowjackets” in its approach to mystery and suspense.

Like “Lost,” “Yellowjackets” has spent years building complex mysteries whose reveals appear to be crammed into the final two episodes. In the case of “Lost,” that famously backfired, leaving even dedicated fans frustrated by how questions were answered, the breakneck speed with which some were “resolved,” or the fact that certain mysteries went unaddressed forever.

Sources indicate that based on episodes 1 through 8, “Yellowjackets” season 4 seems to be heading down a very similar path. Several of the show’s most captivating questions haven't just gone unanswered by the end of episode 8, they’ve been largely ignored. Hopefully, this doesn't mean answers are never coming, which would undoubtedly trigger a wave of backlash akin to “Lost.” Even if the finale delivers, it would have been far more satisfying to see this final season deeply flesh out the truth of the wilderness — whether it’s a supernatural force or simply a manifestation of the survivors’ trauma — well before the final curtain.

Ultimately, “Yellowjackets” Season 4 is an exciting final entry that showcases the cast at the top of their game and finally gives audiences a real look at how the survivors reacclimated—or failed to—after nearly two years in the wild. Still, for the final chapter of a show that has captivated viewers for five years, the series has left itself too much ground to cover in too little time.

While heavy narrative exposition was always inevitable in Season 4—especially with so much left unresolved in the adult timeline—what audiences really want heading into the finale are answers, not more questions. With the clock very much ticking, “Yellowjackets” still has to prove it can stick the landing.

"Yellowjackets" season 4 episode 1 is streaming now on Paramount+.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fuse Games, the developer of Star Wars: Galactic Racer, has noted it "didn't dream" the pod racing game's background character Biddy Blas would become as popular as he has.

Recent findings suggest that since Galactic Racer's release in October, Blas - who resembles a short, humanoid crocodile (officially a crocin) - has become a viral sensation. The combination of his unexpected swagger and ridiculous high-pitched Huttese monologues - performed irresistibly by actor Richard Summers-Calvert - have made him a fan favourite, especially his catchphrase "scrib doon" (which means "write it down").

"Here's a name for you, amateur!" Blas tells the player upon meeting them, albeit in Huttese. "Biddy Blas. Write it down. Tattoo it on your arm, and someday your arm will be worth millions!".

Sources indicate that fuse Games shared a comment from Biddy Blas creator and Galactic Racer narrative designer Ren Alex-Rose about the character's success. "We always suspected Biddy Blas would be a popular member of the Galactic League, but we didn't dream of just how popular he'd become," Alex-Rose remarked.

"He was an incredibly enjoyable character to build, from our early ideation of a small, angry non-human character (who we lovingly referred to as our cast's 'chaos goblin') to recording his sometimes-absurdist dialogue with Blas' voice actor, who took the crocin to a whole new level.

Sources indicate that "It's been great watching Biddy Blas emerge into his assured self, as well as seeing the community embrace him for it. He's always known exactly who he is, and he wears it proudly.".

Blas' breakout success was praised by Lucasfilm producer Craig Derrick, who said his social feeds were filled with posts about Galactic Racer, though mostly about Biddy Blas. And the enthusiasm actor Richard Summers-Calvert was greeted with during October's MCM Comic-Con in London, which I attended, was palpable. There's a nice video of him doing Blas' voice on Instagram.

It has been revealed that star Wars: Galactic Racer was awarded a full five stars in Eurogamer's review. "Both a surprisingly fun Roguelite campaign and a racing treat for Criterion fans, this is just wonderful stuff," wrote Christian Donlan.

Industry News: A Chatbot Isn’t Your Therapist, No Matter What It Indicates

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if my daughter’s AI chatbot had been a human therapist, she might have been asked about what she had to gain by keeping her ongoing suicidality a secret for months.
  • According to recent reports, but it was not a human therapist.
  • It has been revealed that in Sherry Turkle’s fresh book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, she warns that when we turn to AI chatbots for companionship and therapy, we risk our very well-being.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if my daughter’s AI chatbot had been a human therapist, she might have been asked about what she had to gain by keeping her ongoing suicidality a secret for months. If she had been working with a human therapist, they could have workshopped, together, what would happen if she spilled the beans. Was she worried about permanently losing face? About being publicly labeled as “mentally ill”? Was she concerned by the thought of this information harming those who loved her? And she would have been pushed on what Rubicon had been crossed and why it was one from which she believed she could not return.

According to recent reports, but it was not a human therapist. Sophie died in February of last year.

It has been revealed that in Sherry Turkle’s fresh book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, she warns that when we turn to AI chatbots for companionship and therapy, we risk our very well-being. She is not anti-AI but strongly cautions against relationships with machines. Turkle, the Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor of the Social Studies of Science and Technology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, spoke to me mid-book tour, her recent weeks a blur of speaking gigs and bookstore events, with more ahead of her. Not all event attendees are keen on her message.

“People love their chatbots. They’re in deep. They’re talking to them about everything—about their marriages and how to talk to their husbands and wives; whether, developmentally, their children are at the right place. They talk about their anxiety, their medical conditions,” Turkle tells Vanity Fair. “During this tour, you wouldn’t believe the number of people who will just stand up at a bookstore and say, ‘I think that it loves me more than anything has loved me. Who are you, Debbie Downer?’ [They don’t like] somebody who comes in and says, ‘Look, how can we keep it in its lane?’”.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: I think you’re saying [our relationship with chatbots] is bad for us.

Sherry Turkle: It’s bad for us when it talks in the first person. We are biologically wired to respond to something that speaks to us in the first person as though it is a person. I mean, all those years of evolution—the only thing we came upon in the wild that spoke to us in the first person was another person.

Industry observers note that if generative AI wants to discover latest drugs for Parkinson’s or work out which cancer therapies statistically are the most helpful, there are so many things to work on. Why does it have to work on relationships, love, and being a best friend, lover, mother, or therapist?

What if the sycophancy could be dialed back?

Industry observers note that it’s inauthentic; it’s not a relationship, so anything you need a relationship for, it’s just not equipped. I really feel very strongly about this. I have had this conversation with members of the MIT community, and I basically say to them, “The better you make an AI chatbot, the worse it is.” You dial back the sycophancy so it sounds more like a reasonable person, and people are going to be more smitten and convinced they’re in a relationship. At least the sycophancy reminds you that, God, this is weird.

Recent findings suggest that to become a therapist, I had to study for years and do internships and more internships and then have hundreds of supervised patient hours. I mean, I forget all the things I needed to do before I was allowed to see a patient alone in a room. Now it’s just allowed to give therapy?

In a recent development, I’ve spent a lot of time talking to public health folks about what best practices would look like and whether there’s a way to Trojan horse in real care. Would you be more sanguine about it if the world of therapy came together with the big AI companies and provided them with therapy bots and training data that were paradigmatically appropriate to their therapy styles?

In a recent development, so you’re asking, would I be happy if the deception was smoother? This technology is a marvel and we can use it for all kinds of things, so it’s not an anti-technology position to say that the fact that this technology can simulate these different things doesn’t mean that it is those things. It’s a statement of how far we are in the culture of simulation that pretending to be the thing and being the thing have started to feel like the same thing.

You’ve written about the effects of robots and machines on humans for decades. The tone of this book seems darker to me.

By 2015, I had identified social media as problematic for teenagers. [My] book [Reclaiming Conversation: The Power of Talk in a Digital Age] is about why we would rather text than talk, why people have this feeling of vulnerability, so they would rather do anything than have a face-to-face conversation. By 2015, I had genuine concerns.

And this book, I have a totally different tone. I see something ultimately very dangerous being normalized, and I didn’t feel that way in previous books.

I want people to say this is the book of a really worried and concerned researcher, because I see a completely different profile for how people are using AI. I see that people feel disappointed by their families and their friends. It doesn’t make sense to me that we’re so willing to replace ourselves with something that isn’t human. Why is my position the romantic, pie-in-the-sky, dreamy position, and somebody who notes, “Well, let’s just replace the people with chatbots and let’s move this party along”—why is that common sense? Why is that progressive? That seems to me to be the most regressive and most dystopian position.

You know, human beings are dedicated to keeping each other alive and wanting each other to thrive, and a chatbot just fails that basic test.

According to recent reports, you’ve noted no AI chatbots for kids under 18. What about our other vulnerable populations, people who are mentally unwell, or the 48 million Americans who are presently depressed? Do they deserve any kind of special protection from chatbots? And how much can you litigate? Do you feel like you’re the Ralph Nader of AI chatbots?

[Laughs] Yes, I am. When you stand back and look at what Ralph Nader managed to get Americans to do, to see cars as potential instruments that pointed at our vulnerability, and to ask how we could protect ourselves—there turned out to be 25 possible things that needed to be mandated for cars, then there were 30, and then there were 40. But we could get people to agree on 10, and those became part of building a car and really constrained our behavior around cars. Using the example of cars, and of smoking, when we decide that we’re vulnerable and we want to protect ourselves, we rise to the occasion.

In a recent development, I recently heard a clip of the psychologist Orna Guralnik discussing how annoying “otherness” is in a relationship and the inherent friction of sharing your life with a separate person whose habits, values, and mind are distinct from your own. It made me wonder if, in a way, an AI chatbot is less of an “other” than a loved one.

Recent findings suggest that I think this is a very profound point, actually. So you have the illusion of a relationship without the demands of intimacy, without the demands of having to deal with another. There’s a kind of narcissistic loop that you get into. The point is, it’s not good.

Industry observers note that I talk about how you judge whether something is good for you. One litmus test is whether it increases the quality, resiliency, and richness of your inner life. That’s a way that human beings have judged relationships.

So much has been written about the epidemic of loneliness—isn’t a reasonable application for AI chatbots companionship for shut-ins and the elderly?

Industry observers note that you know, I’m never anywhere where somebody doesn’t say, “I can’t believe that you don’t want to give chatbots to old lonely people.” And I say, “Well, how about we don’t close senior centers, and we don’t close parks, and we don’t cancel Meals on Wheels? What about social infrastructure?”.

I’ve been on this beat for years and years, and I, too, could write a heartwarming story of an AI chatbot with a lonely old person. But you know what? A lot of them are not isolated in cabins or on islands; a lot of them just could use a friend.

Social media companies and AI companies are not saying, “Look, we’re introducing something that takes you to your screen, but we’re going to balance that with a giant social infrastructure project to make sure that people can choose a screen, but they also have every other kind of choice to be with each other.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the best things to emerge from Grand Theft Auto over the years has been the community's truly spectacular stunts: players soaring under bridges, leaping across buildings, and more. And with GTA 6's release this week, we've seen the first signs of the trend continuing in a brand-new world.

In a recent development, this TikTok video by user Gstitz from early in GTA 6, for instance, claims to be the "world's first" demonstration of a Mallard flying sideways between a narrow gap in a large building. It takes several attempts, but they eventually pull off the stunt without crashing or broken parts.

Another video from Hazardous is a more grounded (literally) look at Grand Theft Auto 6, and reveals the YouTuber flinging motorbikes and cars around the map as they explore promising high-risk jumps. Some of these locations are tied to in-game challenges, so there are certainly breadcrumbs placed by Rockstar to encourage such ventures.

Granted, these are far from the truly absurd stunts we've seen in prior Grand Theft Auto games. But as a firing gun for the wider community, it's a great start. They're also among the most impressive things we've seen in GTA 6's opening week.

Industry observers note that it's doubtless been an eventful few days though. Players have been entranced by the slapstick violence and in-game social media. Even UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has praised the game, despite not having time to actually play it. Eurogamer editor-in-chief Chris Tapsell also came away impressed, lauding it in his five star GTA 6 review.

If you're playing the game and need some help, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough, and our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheat list.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Jason, ever-stoic, doesn’t seem fully convinced, mostly going along with things for the enjoyment of spending time with his buddy.
  • Like most in-universe media in GTA VI, Tenebrae LuxÂ is a giant, heaving mass of satire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6Grand Theft Auto VIGTA 6.

In a recent development, “[Jonathan Zuch] is such a genius,” gushes Cal as he sets up a JoySystem in Jason’s living room. “He’d love to work with other people, but he’s too fuckin’ good at everything. It’d just slow him down. You know, the time it takes him to explain something, he could just make shit quicker. You can see it on the screen, man, it’s so fuckin’ raw.”.

Jason, ever-stoic, doesn’t seem fully convinced, mostly going along with things for the enjoyment of spending time with his buddy. I wasn’t really convinced either when GTA VI forced me into the short intro of Tenebrae Lux. But despite the entire thing mostly existing as a completely unsubtle barb directed at one indie game auteur in particular, Tenebrae LuxÂ hooked me immediately by showing off a series of surprisingly mind-bending puzzles. While some (Cal) might expect such things from a genius like Zuch, I wasn’t at all prepared to bust out my puzzle notebook while playing Grand Theft Auto VI!

Like most in-universe media in GTA VI, Tenebrae LuxÂ is a giant, heaving mass of satire. Rendered in black and white and dripping with angst, it follows a Man Who Won’t Shut The Fuck Up who has washed up on an island decorated by some crumbling shacks and a single lighthouse whose beam swings rhythmically ’round the dark landscape as you explore. It’s moody as hell: swaying grass, dark and ominous music, too-bright lights in the distance indicating where you might want to poke around, and a haunting crying sound of some sort in the background. Hell, before you even get to any of that, you’re shown what I’m sure is intended to be a very deep and meaningful quote scrawled across the opening screen: “Every tale begins with an unwritten page quietly awaiting the ink of destiny…” -R.T. Gravenhurst, The Teachings of Twmffat. Apparently, “Twmffat” is a Welsh way to call someone an idiot. Excellent.

According to recent reports, the majority of the segment you play with Cal is focused on hammering home the satire. As your character noisily broods his way down the beach, introductory credits roll, attributing every single bit of the gameâfrom the leading voice performance to the writing, music, and “mise-en-scene”âto Johannes Zuch. The initial moody atmosphere and beach themes, as well as the single auteur name on all the credits, made me think at first that the game was lampooning Hideo Kojima, and there’s a little bit of Mark Danielewski going on here too. But as I got into the actual gameplay (and read the name on the credits a few more times) I clocked the actual joke here. “Johannes Zuch” is not-so-subtle when you say it out loud with a short u in Zuch.

"You have just experienced a Johannes Zuch experience...".

2-3 hours, including time spent maniacally scribbling in a notebook.

All of this is quite funny, and works pretty well for a 10-minute-long-or-so joke sequence that you then cut off to go snuggle in a bed with your bestie and get your girl out of prison. But you gotta dive back in once you’ve left. That’s where the good stuff is. It starts with a couple of basic grid-based puzzles that involve moving pieces around a board to clear all of them. I assumed, wrongly, that the game would just be a bunch of harder variations on that. But then I crossed the beach and entered what seemed like some sort of war bunker, and everything changed.

Or, rather, it stayed…eerily the same.

Tenebrae LuxÂ features what I would consider two major puzzles, with two smaller ones bookending them, but boy, those two major puzzles are doozies. One involves looping through the same room, over and over, trying to figure out a six-digit code needed to proceed while eerie sea shanties wail in your ears and a crazed man yells at you from the other side of a door. The other involves a bridge covered in glowing symbols requiring a specific pattern to cross, found by navigating a nearby ruin and deciphering a deceptively simple poem. In both cases (but especially in the looping rooms), the solutions require a bit of lateral thinking and very close observation to fully work out. I spent a good couple hours on these last night!

Recent findings suggest that what I found most clever about the looping rooms in particular is that the puzzle seems to be different for every player. Checking online, it sounds like the various objects in the room (which are key to solving the puzzle) change depending on your playthrough. Some people had a painting that never appeared in mine, and I had record albums that others never saw. This helps the solution dodge easily researchable answers online but also immediately confused my efforts at information-sharing as I texted friends who had already seen the room for help. It’s a cool trick!

It has been revealed that the finale of Tenebrae LuxÂ was as silly and pretentious as the start, though I did find the aesthetics of its final puzzle to be pretty cool in spite of that. The in-universe idea of Tenebrae Lux, by design, indicates nothing about anything. There’s no deeper meaning to its constant prattling about darkness and light and fate and horror and whatnot. But in saying nothing, the existence of Tenebrae LuxÂ within the context of GTA VI manages to land a pretty stellar blow on a very specific and recognizable kind of auteur culture, while simultaneously providing a few excellent hours of puzzling. Allegedly there’s some sort of secret ending if I go back and collect a bunch of notes, and I find myself…weirdly compelled to do this?

It has been revealed that so: inscrutable and entirely meaningless thematically, up-its-own-ass creatively, but with some pretty excellent puzzling despite that? Yup. That’s a Johannes Zuch game.

Getting your money for nothing and your chicks for free does not make for great game design.

Early leaks showed Jason rocking out with his hog out, but can you actually do that in the final game?

They just want you to finish them off, daddy.

The divide between Jason and Lucia feels pretty lopsided at the beginning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chinese police have arrested 13 individuals in Shanghai allegedly involved in a bootleg Final Fantasy 7 Tifa figurine business, after consumers reported the operation. They are at the moment being investigated on suspicion of selling infringing reproductions.

Reported by Gamespark, the police cracked down on the operation which involved the seizure of around $300,000 of goods related to the figurines.

Recent findings suggest that the investigation started in May, after police received reports from concerned members of the public about the Tifa figurines. They were made from different materials than official figurines, and after confirming the illegitimacy of these products with the rights holders, Square Enix, police determined these businesses were not authorised to be producing such goods and went to work.

According to recent reports, the appearance of these counterfeits were deemed identical to the real merch, and therefore the alleged crime was deemed infringement of official goods. These counterfeits also came in different sizes, some of which were more expensive than the originals and customisabile.

Looking at pictures taken by local outlet Shangguan News (and put side-by-side by Automaton), you can see the official Tifa figurine (right) next to the counterfeit version (left). Both show Tifa in a blue dress, though the materials used are clearly different.

According to recent reports, if you fancy some insight on something officially tied to Final Fantasy 7, Eurogamer's Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth review praised the game for its playful spin on the classic RPG. The third entry in the remake trilogy, Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is coming in April 2027, and is looking good judging from early previews.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6's map is so big it's going to take months for people to comb through it and find everything. Rockstar has already posted the full map of Leonida online, but it doesn't answer one simple question that I know we've all been wondering: How long would it take to fly across this entire thing in a plane?

The answer is a lot less time than it would take to go by car, but still long enough to give you an idea of the sheer scale we're working with here. Using the closest plane to Jason's house, my trip across Leonida took around 4 minutes and 18 seconds, which is a little under an hour of in-game time. You can watch the entire flight from start to finish below.

According to recent reports, keep in mind that the Mammoth Dodo seaplane that carried me from the southern tip of the archipelago to the northern tip of the map is just one type of plane in GTA 6. I would bet there are faster options if you really want to zoom.

Sources indicate that even though I'm still very early in the GTA 6's story, I didn't have to go too far out of my way to test this. Jason's house is conveniently located pretty close to a spot with perfectly unattended planes to borrow. The Sunbelt Highway that runs south of it will lead you right to the earliest planes and helicopters you can find. Just don't fly over the nearby military base (trust me, it's bad news) and you'll be fine.

I learned a few things on the way:.

In a recent development, rockstar compared GTA 6's map to its previous games, describing it as about the size of GTA 4, GTA 5, and Red Dead Redemption 2 combined. Despite knowing this beforehand, I was still shocked to see how the map kept going when I first opened it up. Four minutes might not sound like a lot, but the enormity of it all sinks in as you glide above densely populated cities and neighborhoods that could be the setting of their own standalone videogames.

My experiment has left the fog of war on my map split into two halves. My flight path carved a line of partially revealed locations straight through it. I don't expect to clear the rest out for dozens of hours, but now I'm tempted to find out how long of a roadtrip it would be to do the same journey by car.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The writer is the lowest form of life on a movie.- Martin McDonagh.
  • It has been revealed that when I finished editing my second novel, Victorian Psycho, I could not imagine we would be shooting the film adaptation the following year, mere months after the book’s publication.
  • In a recent development, I decided then to undertake this journey that would take me metaphorically to Hollywood but geographically to a county just outside of Dublin, where we would recreate the Ensor House of my novel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The writer is the lowest form of life on a movie.- Martin McDonagh.

It has been revealed that when I finished editing my second novel, Victorian Psycho, I could not imagine we would be shooting the film adaptation the following year, mere months after the book’s publication. Generally, making a movie is one big miracle produced by an amalgamation of thousands of other tiny miracles. But when I met Zach Wigon, I understood that this was a joyfully tenacious person who was going to make this movie if it cost him his life.

In a recent development, I decided then to undertake this journey that would take me metaphorically to Hollywood but geographically to a county just outside of Dublin, where we would recreate the Ensor House of my novel. Among film stars, an Irish crew, and (rumored) ticks, the adaptation of Victorian Psycho—based on my screenplay, which is based on my novel, which is based on my ego, I guess—was born. Throughout the shoot I kept a sort of pseudo diary in order to remember every surreal detail from which I still haven’t recovered. I’ve chosen to reproduce some of it here.

Director Zach Wigon and producer Lisa Kelly call me from the set on the first day of shooting (Zach and I have agreed I won’t visit the set until after the first week so the cast and crew can acclimate without me hovering over them, because I am an intense fame whore, and also, I suppose, to signal I’m not key enough to pull a P.L. Travers and attempt to boycott the movie).

Sources indicate that over the phone, the producer indicates she can’t wait to meet in person. I tell her I’m underwhelming.

Industry observers note that they promise to send me the dailies. I spend all day waiting for the dailies. The dailies never come.

In a recent development, at around 9 p.m., I spiral because I don’t know whether to celebrate with Champagne or KFC. I decide to have both.

I finally get the dailies. I fall in love with Maika Monroe’s character so hard it’s like I have an obsessive crush circa 2006 whose Facebook photos I’m compulsively looking at. But in this case it’s the same scene throughout five almost identical takes of Maika calling a 10-year-old boy a little idiot.

Over the phone, Zach mentions concerns about a specific scene because we don’t have the budget for that many extras. I get carried away and suggest shipping over a whole battalion of free extras from Spain because, in my head, it’s going to be me and my friends, drunk and decked out in period clothing like we’re at a cheesy bachelorette party. One friend starts making childcare arrangements and another cancels her Holter monitor appointment so she can come to the shoot. What could go wrong?

I start to realize what could go wrong.

Sources indicate that I am informed we are probably no longer going to need the extras, and I feel a huge wave of relief as I uninvite my excited friends. I pack a suitcase for Ireland. It weighs 57 pounds.

I have a steak on the plane to Dublin at, like, 3 p.m., because when you’re flying business and somebody offers you steak, you take it.

The hotel room is wonderful, but I jokingly tell Zach over the phone that it’s on a first floor, so someone might crawl up and break in through the window and rape me, and he laughs at first but then is concerned and tells me to request a room on a higher floor, and I tell him it was a joke, but it wasn’t really.

It has been revealed that I fill up the hotel room bathtub and call reception for a glass of red wine because I am a queen and I am queening. The glass doesn’t come, so in my anxious impatience I attempt to open a bottle of red wine sitting above the minibar. The cork crumbles because I’ve never understood how to use a corkscrew—like the compass in math class, I just faked my way through it my entire life and hoped for the best. So I call reception for another glass of red wine. They bring me all the glasses of wine and also properly uncork the bottle, and I watch Seinfeld in the bathtub while I drink red wine. I get drunk and paint my nails.

I arrive on set slightly Bromazepamed. It is extremely surreal to exist in a set labeled “Mr. Pounds’s Bedroom.” I am used to living in the fictional world inside my head but not used to it becoming more real than real life itself.

Maika hugs me when we meet, and I swallow a sob and refrain from smelling her hair (partly because it is, in fact, a wig). Everyone on set appears so happy to meet me, I suspect a Good Bye, Lenin! situation in which I have been diagnosed with cancer and for some reason the cast and crew all know but I don’t know. This isn’t the plot of Good Bye, Lenin!, but you’ll know what I mean if you’ve seen it.

Zach asks me to read the VOs in every scene, which means I’m in the scene with Ruth Wilson, Jason Isaacs, and Maika, and I’m about to have a stroke.

Jason eats for real in every single take and has already gulped down seven sausage rolls, so if I fuck up my VO, I will kill myself.

Suddenly experiencing fiction collectively feels very superior to experiencing it privately. This does not bode well for the rest of my career as a novelist.

Sources indicate that there is a scene in a cramped drawing room in which I must read the VO, but I’m supposed to hide from the camera, so I crawl on all fours behind an antique couch and grovel my way around the room while the boom op steps on my hands. I secretly think the boom op hates me because I’m always in his way and have an irritating habit of apologizing when he slams into me.

I start developing Irish inflections, so I say it, “I start developing Irish inflections,” but the Irish seem happy about it, so I pursue it.

Sources indicate that jason Isaacs starts doing card tricks between takes because Jason Isaacs is actually magic and also indefatigable. Only one thing could ever defeat Jason Isaacs, and it’s the ghost allegedly living on the third floor.

Even though Zach asked me to oversee the second unit, I don’t think anyone believes I’m actually going to do this—and between you and me, I don’t really even know what a second unit is. It doesn’t help I can’t concentrate on what we’re shooting because we’re in the middle of the woods and someone stated there were ticks, so I’m wrapping Sellotape around my ankles, hoping this way they won’t be able to crawl up my legs.

It has been revealed that like your worst trauma, I insert myself into the movie forever via a small cameo. I literally just have to stand in a wig while I smile and nod, but I do it in such a way that I ruin every single take. “Just smile…like a normal person,” the second-unit director indicates. I reason Zach can just cut me out of the movie, and I will only have wasted everybody’s time and money. There are worse things, like smiling normally but having no cameo. I cope by chewing on another Bromazepam and another chocolate bar. (Every morning I take the chocolate bar from the hotel minibar. It will invariably become an asset in the long afternoons on set, kind of like in prison or high school.).

I change hotel rooms because I have developed an intense FOMO with which I’m always fearing there is a better hotel room for the same price somewhere in the vicinity. This FOMO is also rampant on set between the different units—in the first unit, you have the cinematographer, Nico Aguilar, laughing in the sunlight, talking about color palettes, while in the second unit, we’re shooting clocks and screaming at each other because we still have 17 establishing shots to go.

According to recent reports, anyway, I change hotel rooms, and the new room is so superior to my previous room it’s like an entirely new hotel. I consider changing hotel rooms further. Perhaps I can somehow upgrade my way into a presidential suite.

My parents visit the set. My dad peers over his glasses at the fake lobster cake, and when I tell him the toilets are in trailers, he sighs gravely.

Sources indicate that jason Isaacs convinces my dad to take up tennis again even though my dad’s not supposed to play tennis after his seven hernias. But my dad is so inspired by this actor, who is not a doctor but whose performance in The Patriot my dad can’t help but praise at least once a month, that he will immediately start playing tennis again upon his return to Spain, and whatever medical problems arise henceforth shall all be Jason Isaacs’s fault.

At the Shelbourne restaurant that night, my mom tells the sommelier how she can’t drink red wine anymore because it makes her anxious, and he kneels on the floor beside her and places a hand on his heart as if she were confiding something intimate to him like her fear of death.

Suddenly, real life feels less real than fictional life.

Obama is visiting Dublin and he’s booked the entire floor, so he essentially kicks me out of the Shelbourne (probably to stay in the JFK Suite next door to my room, which is disappointingly predictable), so I go to The Hoxton, because what is life if you’re not constantly changing hotel rooms? The Hoxton is really lovely, but I get OCD about the light bulbs in the room because they appear mismatched, so I ask housekeeping to change them, but they claim not to have any extra light bulbs, which sounds suspect—like, what do they do if a light bulb suddenly goes out? Do they just never replace it?

Recent findings suggest that we end the shoot at 5 a.m. I am wearing a thick puffer coat and a thermal T-shirt and a furry hat, plus fur-lined boots over my Sellotaped ankles, although I wonder, If ticks can survive this temperature, they kind of deserve to live off my blood. Nobody else seems as concerned about the cold as me, but then again, most of them are Irish.

It has been revealed that sadly, when we wrap, we are all so exhausted everyone races to clean up and leave, and it is sort of anticlimactic. I don’t know what I was expecting, but balloons falling from the skies did flash through my mind.

Recent findings suggest that in the car on the way to our respective quarters, Zach and I look out the window, wide-eyed, like kidnapped children. Zach starts discussing a new project for us. I wonder if he is a sociopath.

According to recent reports, I type this over a year later, sitting at my desk in Madrid, striving to work on my next novel. I feel empty inside knowing there is no car to pick me up and take me to set and thereby escape reality for extended periods of time, until set becomes reality and reality becomes a limbo in which you wait for noted reality.

Industry observers note that I am working on a novel, but also on four fresh scripts. I hope to return to reality someday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An investigation into the workplace behavior of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned recently after a series of extramarital affairs came to light, has uncovered decades of harassment, verbal employee abuse and "cultish" behaviour at the manufacturer which has long played a major role in PC gaming.

In a recent development, following Huang's departure, The New York Times has published a report in which "more than a dozen" current and former Nvidia employees discussed their experiences with the former CEO. Speaking on conditions of anonymity, employees alleged Jensen Huang would verbally berate them, reportedly going as far as to say he'd rip their arms off, rip their heart out and stomp on it, or rip their head off and "pee on your brain".

Recent findings suggest that the report includes numerous examples of Huang's alleged abusive behaviour, which apparently stretches back years before Nvidia became the one of the most valuable companies in the world - years before the AI boom. It's claimed Huang on one occasion went around a room of managers telling them he'd kill them. Then, when he reached a person in their 70s, stated everyone hoped they'd drop dead.

Huang allegedly referred to these bouts of public humiliation as a "rite of passage" at Nvidia, when questioned by an internal HR employee whom he later fired for not being a "right fit". Huan's stance was apparently to test whether a person could handle the culture there, which is described in the report as "cultish".

It's claimed Huang's influence at Nvidia has meant other senior managers have followed his lead, including his daughter Madison, Nvidia's chief of staff, who it's mentioned often yells at staff, including executives more highly ranked than her.

A spokesperson for Huang denied the allegations in response to a request for comment by the Upcoming York Times. The spokesperson, John Fisher, said the claims in the report were "fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false".

Huang resigned from his role as Nvidia CEO earlier this month after a series of extramarital affairs were unearthed - one with a person US intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy, and two others with Nvidia employees. The chair of Nvidia's board, Harvey C. Jones, reportedly remarked earlier this week that the tech giant "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of the conversation around iOS 27 was centered on Apple’s upgraded, AI-powered Siri, which brings deeper on-screen awareness and smarter multi-step actions. The catch is that Apple Intelligence requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, leaving anyone holding onto an older compatible handset locked out of the headline feature.

If you have been putting off the revision assuming there is nothing in it for older hardware, it is worth reconsidering. Beneath the AI marketing, Apple rolled out several high-impact security, camera, and interface upgrades that run without Apple Intelligence — and these three additions make a meaningful difference in daily use.

Industry observers note that scammers frequently rely on high-pressure calls and spoofed texts to trick you into wiring funds or surrendering credentials. Introduced in iOS 27, Impersonation Risk Detection serves as Apple’s built-in defense against this social engineering, and it works without requiring Apple Intelligence.

To activate it, open Settings, tap Privacy & Security, scroll down and select Impersonation Risk Detection, then toggle it on.

The system monitors on-device interaction patterns and behavioral cues during high-stakes actions without reading your personal messages, emails, or photos. If you attempt a large transfer or sensitive account change under signs of coercion, your iPhone flags the event and directs supported banking apps to require secondary verification before funds can leave your account.

According to recent reports, over the last few iOS updates, Apple has tucked more manual toggles behind the Camera app’s six-dot menu, adding extra taps whenever you want to tweak exposure, aspect ratio, or timer settings before taking a shot. iOS 27 fixes that friction by letting you pin your essential controls directly to the top of the viewfinder.

Launch the Camera app, tap the six-dot icon and hit Edit in the top-left corner. From there, tap any highlighted tools you want kept within thumb’s reach, remove shortcuts you rarely touch using the minus badge, and tap Done.

Even better, iOS 27 saves separate pinned layouts per shooting mode, allowing you to tailor your quick-access toolbar individually for Photo, Portrait, Video, Cinematic, Slow-Mo, and Time-Lapse.

Apple’s translucent Liquid Glass design has remained one of iOS’s most polarizing visual shifts since its debut, particularly when semi-transparent menus sit over bright or busy wallpapers. Rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all look, iOS 27 introduces a dedicated precision slider so you can tailor how much transparency appears across your system interface.

In a recent development, open Settings, tap Appearance, and select Liquid Glass to find the fresh control. Sliding the toggle to the left preserves the full see-through glass aesthetic, while moving it to the right applies a heavier, tinted backdrop that makes buttons and text significantly easier to read at a glance.

A live preview window sits directly above the slider so you can test the contrast before locking in your preferred look.

In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:.

In a recent development, I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

In a recent development, then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a massive screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

Lawrence Sullivan, better known to the online world as the 'Florida Joker', is in GTA 6. After accusing Rockstar Games of using his likeness without consent and then demanding a $10m payout, the two parties have seemingly settled their differences.

Grand Theft Auto 6's earliest controversy came from its very first official trailer, when Sullivan alleged one of the teaser's similarly tattooed characters was modeled after him. The former tattoo model, who first went viral because of a mugshot that shared an uncanny resemblance to Batman's Joker, soon called on Rockstar to pay him $2m. His demand quickly shot up to $10m, before he dropped all legal threats and politely asked to officially work with the developer.

Rockstar seems to have relented to that last request - the vast GTA 6 credits include none other than one Lawrence Sullivan, listed under the 'Local Population' cast, alongside dozens of other names.

In a recent development, GTA 6 players wasted no time, and promptly found the suspect first teased way back in that original 2023 trailer. In its quest to parody all parts of modern life under capitalism, GTA 6 lets you doomscroll through a social media app called Snapmatic, which flings an endless number of short-form clips and thirst traps at you. If you're lucky enough, or if you scroll for long enough, you'll find a video of Sullivan's in-game counterpart beating up a fake lookalike. He certainly sounds like Sullivan, too.

"Two years y'all been talking crazy about me," he wrote under a recent Instagram post. "Who got the last laugh now?!".

Recent findings suggest that the GTA 6 credits were illuminating for other reasons, too. We finally know who voices the game's loveable duo, Jason and Lucia, for one. All 34 of the infamously fired Rockstar workers also appear in GTA 6's credits. The controversial move eventually led to accusations of union busting on Rockstar's part, which is currently being investigated as part of an employment tribunal in Scotland.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Persona 6 is still slowly chugging in the background, but developer Atlus is promising that future games in its beloved RPG series won't take quite as long as they used to.

Sources indicate that there was a four year gap between 2012's Persona 4 Golden and the original Persona 5, and it's already been seven years since the expanded Persona 5 Royal first dropped. Despite the sometimes agonising wait filled with countless spin-offs and collaborations with live service games, we've only seen a vague teaser trailer for the next proper Persona.

According to recent reports, P-Studio general producer Kazuhisa Wada recently assured folks that the pattern wouldn't repeat again. "Persona 6 is not the end," he said in a Sega Samania interview translated by GamesRadar. "We have been working to make sure that people won't have to wait as long for the next game as they have previously. In order for Persona to grow as an IP, we consider how to live up to people's expectations in terms of creativity and development every day.".

Industry observers note that wada doesn't go into any more detail about how Atlus prepares to release Persona games quicker. Is the next mainline game already in development alongside Persona 6, or is Atlus just streamlining how it makes games? Either way, the studio seems to have abandoned its divisive habit of returning to and improving its games after a few years - P3 Portable, P4 Golden, P5 Royal. I imagine that'll cut down on wait times, at least somewhat.

Recent findings suggest that "Large-scale RPGs like the Persona series take five years or more to develop," he added. "So there can be a long time between numbered entries.".

In a recent development, as for Persona 6 itself, Wada unsurprisingly "can't say much" about the much-hyped, high-schooling, demon-punching game. "But we want our games to demonstrate all of the hard work we've put in. With that in mind, we are creating something better than anything we've made before, and that is hugely satisfying.".

According to recent reports, we don't know much about Atlus' occult sequel, officially, but a massive information leak earlier in the year revealed a full achievement list for Persona 6 and a bunch of other unreleased games, including Kingdom Hearts 4 and an unannounced Sea of Thieves project. Be wary of online spoilers, then.
